section_summary: This final section consists chiefly of public protests against American exports of arms, aircraft, scrap iron, trucks, gasoline, and other supplies to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War, together with State Department replies. Church representatives, college faculty, and educators argued that the trade made the United States complicit in Japan’s aggression against China; the Department repeatedly answered that the Neutrality Act could halt only arms exports, and only after a presidential proclamation that would embargo both belligerents. The replies also cite export-license totals and, in one case, note the virtual cessation of aircraft-related licenses to countries bombing civilian populations.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning Lloyd L. Farley’s protest against exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The Department proposes a legal and policy explanation for responding to Lloyd L. Farley’s protest against exports of war and other materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter explains that a presidential finding of war under the Neutrality Act would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, while no statutory authority existed to stop them without such a proclamation. It adds that the act did not cover commodities outside the official munitions list and cites arms-export licenses worth about $14.37 million for China and $10.79 million for Japan. Because the United States had condemned aerial bombing of civilians, licensing of aircraft and aircraft supplies to countries engaged in such bombing had virtually ceased.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing a Mount Vernon petition against the arms traffic
subfiles.about: A Mount Vernon pastor submits a petition seeking an end to the war and changes to American arms-traffic laws.
subfiles.summary: Custis asks Hull to consider an enclosed petition urging him to use his influence to end the war between Japan and China. He particularly calls for revision of American arms-traffic laws so that the United States will not become a partner in the Far Eastern conflict.

subfiles.title: Mount Vernon petition against war-sustaining trade with Japan
subfiles.from: S. K. Custis and other Mount Vernon petitioners
subfiles.about: Christian petitioners urge Hull to end American commerce that sustains Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that trade with Japan makes the United States a partner in the destruction of Chinese lives and property. Its Christian signatories describe a sense of guilt over American complicity and appeal for government action. The petition is followed by numerous handwritten signatures, many of which are poorly captured by the OCR.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to S. K. Custis
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the Mount Vernon petition and explains the legal limits of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that an embargo under the Neutrality Act required a presidential proclamation that a state of war existed, and that the resulting embargo would apply to both China and Japan. He explains that the President exercised statutory discretion not to issue such a proclamation and that the act did not authorize restrictions on commodities outside the official munitions list. The letter reports licensed arms exports of roughly $14.28 million to China and $10.79 million to Japan and encloses the Joint Resolution and a pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Lindsey Blayney’s protest against supplies for Japan
subfiles.about: Carleton College’s dean protests further shipments capable of prolonging Japan’s war against China.
subfiles.summary: Blayney vehemently opposes continued shipments of supplies usable in Japan’s war against China. He says such exports should stop even if doing so risks involving the United States in war.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Lindsey Blayney
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department answers Blayney’s protest with its standard explanation of the Neutrality Act and export figures.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential proclamation recognizing a state of war would stop arms exports to both China and Japan, whereas no statutory authority existed without one. He says the President’s decision reflected the act’s purpose of keeping the United States out of war and notes that non-munitions commodities could not be prohibited under the law. The letter cites licensed arms exports of approximately $14.28 million to China and $10.79 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: George W. Hinman’s appeal for an embargo and diplomatic action against Japan
subfiles.about: A Foochow College official urges the United States to end trade with Japan and make a forceful diplomatic protest against Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Hinman condemns American profits from exports of scrap iron, trucks, aircraft, and gasoline used in the killing of Chinese people. He warns that Japan’s proposed “new order” and rejection of the Open Door threaten American trade, democratic ideals, philanthropic work, and friendship with China. He advocates withdrawing the ambassador and imposing a comprehensive embargo, praises Admiral Yarnell’s conduct in China, and asks that the President follow the October protest with further diplomatic action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to George W. Hinman
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Hinman’s views and outlines the Neutrality Act’s limited authority over exports.
subfiles.summary: Green assures Hinman that his views on the Far East have received careful attention. He explains that a presidential war proclamation would embargo arms shipments to both China and Japan, and that the Neutrality Act did not empower the government to prohibit other commodities. The reply reports arms-export licenses of approximately $14.28 million for China and $10.79 million for Japan and encloses the Joint Resolution and explanatory pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Geneva District Conference protest against shipments to aggressor nations
subfiles.about: A Methodist conference reports its unanimous protest against exporting war materials to Japan or any aggressor nation.
subfiles.summary: Carpenter reports that the Geneva District Conference, meeting at Waterloo on November 18, unanimously voted to protest to the President and Secretary of State. The resolution opposed shipment of any kind of war material from the United States to Japan or another aggressor nation. Carpenter states that the conference represented sixty-five churches with 13,000 members.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to J. R. Carpenter
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the Methodist resolution and explains why the Neutrality Act had not stopped exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green thanks Carpenter for reporting the Geneva District Conference’s unanimous resolution. He says that only a presidential proclamation could activate an arms embargo and that the measure would apply equally to China and Japan. The reply further explains that the law did not cover non-munitions commodities and cites licensed exports of about $14.28 million to China and $10.79 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning the Mount Holyoke College faculty resolution
subfiles.from: Francis B. Sayre, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds to Warbeke’s letter and a Mount Holyoke faculty resolution concerning the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Sayre acknowledges Warbeke’s November 20 letter and a resolution signed by members of the Mount Holyoke College faculty. He repeats that the Neutrality Act required a presidential proclamation before arms exports could be barred and that any resulting embargo would cover both China and Japan. The letter also emphasizes that the statute did not reach other commodities and supplies the familiar export-license totals for the two belligerents.
